bib.title: Introduction to Information Retrieval, Chapter 18: Matrix decompositions and latent semantic indexing
bib.venue: Cambridge University Press (online edition, DRAFT April 1, 2009, book pp. 403-419)

question: How can the SVD of the term-document matrix give a low-rank representation (latent semantic indexing) that copes with synonymy and polysemy in retrieval?
hypothesis: Squeezing terms and documents into k dimensions brings together terms with similar co-occurrences, so retrieval quality should not suffer much and may improve.

results.claim: Eckart-Young: the best rank-k approximation under Frobenius norm is the truncated SVD Ck, with error equal to the (k+1)th singular value.

limits: No experiments of its own: all effectiveness evidence is second-hand from Dumais (1993, 1995) on TREC in the early 1990s, with no precision/recall numbers printed.
Dated (2008): the one-million-document ceiling and the day-long SVD are superseded; randomised/sparse SVD, learned dense embeddings, and neural retrievers are not covered.
LSI shares vector-space drawbacks: no negation, no Boolean conditions (p. 417).
The authors say LSI has not been established as a significant force in scoring and ranking (p. 403).
Full proof of Theorem 18.3 and detailed derivations are declared out of scope.
Folding-in ignores co-occurrences and new terms of added documents, so quality degrades (p. 414).

Internal inconsistencies: the chapter intro says LSI is in Section 18.3 and low-rank approximations in 18.2, but they are 18.4 and 18.3; exercises 18.8 and 18.9 refer to 'Example 18.12' and 'Exercise 18.13', which should be Example 18.3 and Exercise 18.5 (equation 18.12/18.13 numbers merged into the references); Exercise 18.1 calls its non-diagonal matrix a 'diagonal matrix'; the matrix labelled C2 in Example 18.4 is actually Sigma'_2 V'^T (the truncated document matrix, identical to the printed (V')^T), not U Sigma_k V^T.
practices: Choose k far smaller than the rank of C, in the low hundreds in the cited experiments (p. 413).
Map queries into LSI space with q_k = Sigma_k^-1 U_k^T q and score with cosine similarity (pp. 413-414).
To scale LSI, build it on a random sample of documents and fold in the rest (p. 416).
Recompute the LSI representation once enough documents have been folded in (p. 414).
Use the reduced (truncated) SVD with k columns/rows to avoid multiplying by zeros (p. 412).
LSI works best where queries and documents overlap little (p. 417).

terms.definition: The rank of a matrix is the number of linearly independent rows (or columns) in it
values of λ satisfying C x = λ x

S = Q Λ Q^T with orthonormal eigenvector columns (Theorem 18.2)
C = U Σ V^T, U from eigenvectors of C C^T, V from eigenvectors of C^T C, σi = sqrt(λi) (Theorem 18.3)
Written form with Σ as r x r and omitted zero columns/rows of U and V
Ck of rank at most k minimising Frobenius norm of C - Ck, with k far smaller than r
Cast documents and queries into the low-rank SVD representation and compute query-document similarity there; also called LSA
